measurement: realised invocation cost of batched verification, and why isolation is a flat fall-back rather than a bisection
why: LL.md 29.13's follow-up left isolation unmeasured and asserted a bisection would be cheaper than re-running every candidate. Measuring it refuted that: with ~97% of an invocation fixed, each bisection branch re-pays nearly a whole verification.
conclusion: Bisection cost 11 and 15 invocations at 2 and 4 failures of 8, against 8 for plain individual runs and a flat 9 for batch-then-fall-back. The flat strategy is shipped. Batching is 8x only at a 100% acceptance rate and is a net loss from two failures in eight onward, so the break-even acceptance rate is roughly 75-88% -- NOT the 84% failure rate an earlier incorrect calculation gave. An evolutionary search where most candidates fail is the regime in which batching costs more than verifying one at a time.
not_established: One run per scenario; invocation counts are exact, wall-clock is a single sample.
n=8 only. A larger batch raises the all-pass saving and does not change the break-even logic.
A persistent Lean server was never built; this is batching into one file as the cheap approximation of process reuse.

cost_model.note: The measured rows fix the number of failures, so they are CONDITIONAL costs. Over many batches at a per-candidate failure rate p, some batches pass entirely, so the expected cost is more favourable than the conditional-on-failure row suggests. This model is the honest reading and it changes the conclusion.
cost_model.conclusion: Conditional on a batch containing a failure, batching costs about 12% more than individual runs. In EXPECTATION it still pays while (1-p)^b > 1/b: at b=8 that is a failure rate below about 24%, and the optimal batch size falls as the failure rate rises. So batching is worth having for a gate with a high acceptance rate and the batch size must be tuned to the realised acceptance rate -- it is not a free win and at a 50% failure rate no batch size above 2 helps.
